Abstract
Motivated by the FPTAS for connectivity interdiction of Huang et al. [4], we isolate the part of the
argument that does not use cuts. The setting is a minimization problem over a feasible-set family F with a
linear objective w(S) =
P
e∈S w(e). After dualizing the interdiction budget, deletion can be absorbed into
truncated weights wλ(e) = min{w(e),λc(e)}. At an optimal Lagrange multiplier λ∗, the unknown optimal
interdiction witness is a strict 2-approximate minimizer of the reweighted problem. Thus an exact algorithm
can be obtained whenever one can optimize wλ∗over F, enumerate all its 2-approximate minimizers, and
solve the remaining knapsack problem.

The set S is the object chosen by the original minimization problem, and R is the part of S removed by the
interdiction budget. For a fixed S, choosing R is a knapsack-like deletion problem; the global difficulty is that
we do not know which feasible set S will be optimal after deletion.

Therefore we have L(λ) = minS∈F wλ(S), which is the original linear optimization problem under the truncated

The function Φ is the lower envelope of finitely many lines in λ, so it is piecewise-linear and concave.
Lemma 2.1 For every λ ≥0, Φ(λ) ≤OPT. Hence Λ ≤OPT.
Proof: Let (S,R) be feasible for (1). Since c(R) ≤b, w(S \ R) + λ(c(R) −b) ≤w(S \ R). Minimizing the
left-hand side over all pairs (S,R), and then minimizing the right-hand side only over budget-feasible pairs,
gives Φ(λ) ≤OPT.
□
Lemma 2.2 Assume λ∗is a finite maximizer of Φ. Then there is a pair (SLD,RLD) attaining L(λ∗) such that
c(RLD) ≤b. Consequently,
L(λ∗) ≥OPT.
Proof: If every pair attaining L(λ∗) had c(R) > b, then every active line in the lower envelope defining Φ
would have positive slope at λ∗. For sufficiently small δ > 0, the value of the lower envelope would then
increase from λ∗to λ∗+ δ, contradicting the optimality of λ∗.
Thus some active pair (SLD,RLD) has c(RLD) ≤b. This pair is feasible for (1), so w(SLD \ RLD) ≥OPT.
Therefore
L(λ∗) = w(SLD \ RLD) + λ∗c(RLD) ≥OPT.
□

4
Algorithmic template
The theorem gives the a general template shown in Figure 4.1. λ∗can be found using parametric search
techniques.
Lemma 4.1 ( [7]) Let S(n) be the complexity of computing L(λ) = minH∈F wλ(H) for fixed λ (where n is the
size of the input), then one can compute λ∗using parametric search in O(S(n)2) time.
If there is a parallel algorithm that solves L(λ) for fixed λ using P(n) processors in time T(n), then one can
compute λ∗using parametric search in O(S(n)T(n)log P(n) + T(n)P(n)) time.
Computing gb(S) is essentially solving a knapsack problem on groundset S and takes ˜O(m + 1
ϵ2 ) time for
an (1 + ϵ)-approximation [2]. This algorithmic template shows the interdiction version of a minimization
problem can be reduced to polynomially many knapsack problem if all strict 2-approximations of a reweighted
original problem can be enumerated in polynomial time.
4.1
Application on Connectivity Interdiction
Let G = (V, E) be an undirected multigraph, and let F be the family of all nontrivial cuts δ(U), where ; ̸= U ⊊V.
The interdiction problem is
min
C∈F, R⊆C
c(R)≤b
w(C \ R).
If there is a cut C with c(C) ≤b, then the optimum is 0: remove all edges in C. This case is detected by one
min-cut computation under capacities c, so below assume every cut has c-cost larger than b.
For a fixed λ, put capacity wλ(e) = min{w(e),λc(e)} on every edge. Then L(λ) = minC∈F wλ(C), so
evaluating L(λ) is just a global min-cut computation in (G, wλ). Using the deterministic almost-linear time
min-cut algorithm of Li [6], this takes ˜O(m) time. Therefore, Lemma 4.1 gives a ˜O(m2)-time algorithm for
computing λ∗. If randomization is allowed, we can find λ∗in near linear time. Min-cut can be computed with
high probability in O(mlog2 n) work and O(log3 n) depth [1]. Brent’s law [3] shows that the running time is
T(n, P) = O( mlog2 n
P
+ log3 n) with P processors. Setting P = O(m) and plugging the parallel algorithm into
Lemma 4.1 give a randomized ˜O(m)-time algorithm for λ∗.
Let L∗= L(λ∗). By Theorem 3.1, the optimal interdiction cut C∗satisfies wλ∗(C∗) < 2L∗. Thus C∗is one of
the strict 2-approximate min-cuts in (G, wλ∗). Karger [5] showed that the number of α-approximate min-cuts is
O(n⌊2α⌋). Hence the number of cuts with value strictly smaller than 2L∗is O(n3), and they can be enumerated
in randomized O(n3) time1 [5]. To sum up, our framework gives an FPRAS for connectivity interdiction with
running time ˜O(m + n3(m + 1
ϵ2 )).
Compared with [4], our analyais is based on LP methods and is more intuitive. An algorithmic improvement
is that we use parametric search thus avoiding the enumeration of λ∗(the optimum of a normalized min-cut
problem in [4]).

Abstract: Motivated by the FPTAS for connectivity interdiction of Huang et al. [4], we isolate the part of the argument that does not use cuts. The setting is a minimization problem over a feasible-set family F with a linear objective w(S) = P e∈S w(e). After dualizing the interdiction budget, deletion can be absorbed into truncated weights wλ(e) = min{w(e),λc(e)}. At an optimal Lagrange multiplier λ∗, the unknown optimal interdiction witness is a strict 2-approximate minimizer of the reweighted problem. Thus an exact algorithm can be obtained whenever one can optimize wλ∗over F, enumerate all its 2-approximate minimizers, and solve the remaining knapsack problem.
